deep.title: Quorum math with worked examples
deep.body:
N replicas, a write waits for W acks, a read contacts R replicas. If R + W > N, every read set overlaps every write set in at least one replica, so a read sees at least one copy of the latest acknowledged write (when versions are compared correctly).

Examples with N = 3:

- R = 2, W = 2: overlap of 1. Tolerates 1 node down for reads and writes. Balanced default.
- R = 1, W = 3: fast reads, writes fail if any node is down.
- R = 3, W = 1: fast writes, slow reads, reads fail if any node is down.
- R = 1, W = 1: R + W = 2 <= 3, so stale reads are possible. Fastest, eventual.

Fault tolerance: writes survive N − W failures; reads survive N − R failures.

Latency: an operation completes when the W-th (or R-th) fastest replica responds, so latency is an order statistic. Larger quorums raise tail latency.

Why R + W > N is not full linearizability: sloppy quorums and hinted handoff accept writes on nodes outside the preference list during failures; a write that reaches W nodes may later be overwritten by a concurrent write with an older timestamp (last-write-wins with clock skew); a read concurrent with a write can see new then old values on successive reads. Add read repair and real consensus if you need strict guarantees.

Conflict handling: version vectors (each replica increments its own counter; if neither vector dominates the other the writes are concurrent and both siblings are kept), dotted version vectors, or CRDTs. LWW by timestamp is simple but silently drops one of two concurrent writes.

deep.title: Repair mechanisms in leaderless stores
deep.body:
Read repair: when a read sees replicas disagree, the coordinator writes the newest version back to stale replicas.

Hinted handoff: if a replica is down during a write, another node stores a hint and delivers it when the replica returns. Improves write availability (sloppy quorum) but weakens the overlap guarantee.

Anti-entropy: background comparison of replicas using Merkle trees (hash of hash ranges) to find and sync differing key ranges efficiently, transferring only the differences.

Tunable per request: Cassandra offers ONE, QUORUM, LOCAL_QUORUM (quorum within the local datacenter, avoiding cross-region latency), EACH_QUORUM, ALL. A common production setting is LOCAL_QUORUM for both reads and writes.

flows.title: Raft: election then replicated write
flows.hint: Five steps from a dead leader to a committed entry.

steps.note: Follower hears no heartbeat for a randomized timeout (150-300 ms, randomized to avoid split votes)
It becomes a candidate, increments its term, votes for itself and asks the others for votes
A node grants its vote once per term, only if the candidate's log is at least as up to date as its own
With a majority of votes the candidate becomes leader and starts sending heartbeats
Client write: leader appends the entry to its log and sends AppendEntries to followers
A majority has stored the entry: it is committed. Leader applies it and replies to the client
Followers learn the commit index in the next heartbeat and apply the entry to their state machines

deep.title: The three sub-problems of Raft
deep.body:
Leader election: terms are logical clocks. Each node is follower, candidate or leader. A leader sends heartbeats; a follower that times out starts an election. A node votes at most once per term and only for a candidate whose log is at least as up to date (higher last term, or equal term and longer log). Randomized timeouts make split votes rare and quickly resolved. At most one leader per term because it needs a majority.

Log replication: the leader appends client commands to its log and replicates with AppendEntries. Each message carries the index and term of the previous entry (consistency check). If a follower's log differs, the leader walks back to the last matching entry and overwrites the follower's conflicting suffix. An entry is committed once stored on a majority; the leader only counts replicas for entries of its own term (the safety rule that prevents committing old-term entries through a count alone).

Safety: Leader Completeness (any committed entry is present in the log of every future leader) follows from the up-to-date vote rule plus majority overlap: a candidate cannot win without a vote from at least one node holding every committed entry.

Cluster sizing: a cluster of N = 2f + 1 nodes tolerates f failures. 3 nodes tolerate 1, 5 tolerate 2. Even sizes add cost without extra tolerance.

Performance: each write needs one round trip to a majority, so latency is the median replica's latency; batching and pipelining raise throughput. Linearizable reads need either going through the log, a read index (leader confirms leadership with a heartbeat round), or leader leases (relying on bounded clock drift).

Membership changes and snapshots: reconfigure with joint consensus or single-server changes; compact the log with snapshots so it does not grow forever and new nodes can catch up.

deep.title: Raft vs Paxos vs ZAB, and where consensus is used
deep.body:
Paxos: the original, proven protocol; notoriously hard to implement fully (multi-Paxos details are underspecified). Raft was designed for understandability with the same guarantees. ZAB (ZooKeeper) is similar to Raft with primary-backup ordering semantics.

Used for: metadata and coordination stores (etcd for Kubernetes, ZooKeeper, Consul), distributed databases per shard or range (Spanner uses Paxos groups, CockroachDB and TiKV use Raft per range), leader election, distributed locks and configuration.

Not used for: bulk data paths with huge throughput without sharding the groups; cross-continent synchronous writes unless you accept 100+ ms commit latency. Multi-Raft shards the data across many small Raft groups to scale.

deep.title: What CAP actually says (and PACELC)
deep.body:
Consistency here means linearizability. Availability means every request to a non-failing node gets a non-error response. Partition tolerance means the system keeps operating when the network drops messages between nodes. Since partitions happen in real networks, the real choice is: during a partition, give up consistency (answer, maybe stale: AP) or availability (refuse or wait: CP).

Common mistakes: treating it as 'pick 2 of 3' (you cannot choose to forgo partitions), labeling whole databases, or applying it to a single node.

PACELC extends it: if there is a Partition choose between Availability and Consistency; Else (normal operation) choose between Latency and Consistency. Even with no partition, replicating synchronously for consistency costs latency. Examples: Dynamo/Cassandra are PA/EL by default; Spanner and most consensus systems are PC/EC; MongoDB defaults are PA/EC in some configurations; many relational primary-replica setups are PC/EC for the primary and EL when reading from async replicas.

How to answer in an interview: pick per feature. Payments and inventory decrement: CP behavior (reject or queue if not sure). Feed, likes, presence: AP behavior (serve something). Then name the mechanism (quorum, leader with sync follower, CRDT) and what the user sees during a partition.

flows.title: Order saga with compensation
flows.hint: Payment fails at step 3, earlier steps are undone in reverse.

steps.note: T1: order created in PENDING state (local transaction commits)
T2: stock reserved (reservation row with expiry)
T3: payment declined. The saga cannot continue
C2: compensate by releasing the reservation (idempotent)
C1: mark the order CANCELLED and notify the customer. The final state is consistent

deep.title: Orchestration vs choreography, and designing the steps
deep.body:
Orchestration: a central coordinator (a workflow engine like Temporal, Step Functions or a saga table) tells each service what to do and records state. Easy to see the whole flow, handle timeouts and retries, and add steps; the orchestrator is an extra component that must be highly available and must not contain business logic that belongs in services.

Choreography: services react to each other's events. No central point, loose coupling, but the flow is implicit across services, hard to trace, and cyclic dependencies creep in. Fine for 2 or 3 steps.

Step design rules:

- Every step has a compensating action (or is the last step). Compensation is a semantic undo (refund, release), not a database rollback; the intermediate state was visible to others.
- Steps and compensations must be idempotent and retriable until success.
- Order steps so that the hardest-to-undo or most likely to fail comes early, and irreversible ones (sending an email, shipping) come last. A pivot transaction is the point after which the saga must go forward.
- Use semantic locks and pending states (PENDING, RESERVED) so other transactions see in-progress data correctly.
- Persist saga state before each step so a crash resumes instead of starting over; handle a timeout as failure with compensation.

Isolation problems (no ACID I): lost updates, dirty reads and non-repeatable reads across saga steps. Countermeasures: semantic locks, commutative updates, version checks, reread values, and putting the risky step first.

deep.title: Isolation anomalies with examples
deep.body:
Dirty read: reading uncommitted data of another transaction (prevented by read committed and above).

Non-repeatable read: read a row twice and it changed in between (prevented by snapshot isolation).

Phantom: re-running a range query returns new rows (prevented by serializable, or by snapshot isolation for reads).

Lost update: two transactions read-modify-write the same value and one write is overwritten. Fix: atomic update (SET x = x + 1), SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, or compare-and-set with a version column.

Write skew: two transactions read overlapping data, make disjoint writes based on it and together break an invariant (two on-call doctors both go off-call; two bookings for the same room slot). Snapshot isolation allows it. Fix: serializable isolation, SELECT FOR UPDATE on the rows read, or a database constraint.

How serializability is implemented: two-phase locking (pessimistic, readers block writers), serial execution (single thread per partition, as in Redis or VoltDB), or serializable snapshot isolation (optimistic, detect dangerous patterns and abort one transaction, as in Postgres). Under SSI clients must retry aborted transactions.

deep.title: Locking strategies compared
deep.body:
Atomic conditional update: UPDATE inventory SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = ? AND qty > 0, then check rows affected. One statement, no lock held by the client, no race. Best first choice for counters and stock.

Pessimistic locking: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks the row until commit. Safe under high contention; holds locks (blocking, deadlock risk, lower throughput). Keep transactions short and always lock in a consistent order.

Optimistic concurrency control: read a version, write with WHERE version = ?; if 0 rows updated, retry. No locks; wasted work under contention, so use when conflicts are rare.

Distributed lock (Redis SET NX PX, ZooKeeper, etcd): mutual exclusion across processes. Always set a lease/TTL so a dead holder releases it. A paused holder can wake after its lease expired and still write, so protect the resource with a fencing token (a monotonically increasing number the resource checks and rejects if stale). Redlock's safety is debated; for correctness use a consensus-backed lock with fencing.

Single-writer queue: serialize all updates for a key through one consumer (partition by key). Removes contention entirely at the cost of latency and a queue.

Deadlocks: two transactions wait on each other. Databases detect and abort one; prevent by lock ordering, timeouts and short transactions.

deep.title: Hot rows and high-contention counters
deep.body:
A single row updated thousands of times per second serializes on its lock. Options: shard the counter into N rows (increment a random one, sum on read), buffer increments in memory or a queue and flush batches, use a counter service, or accept approximate counts (probabilistic counters).

Flash sale pattern: put a virtual waiting room or queue in front, admit users at a rate the inventory service can handle, reserve stock with expiring holds, confirm on payment, release on expiry. Avoids a thundering herd on one hot row.

steps.note: Normal: calls flow, failures and slow calls are counted in a sliding window
Failure rate exceeds the threshold (for example 50% of the last 20 calls, minimum 10 calls)
Breaker opens. Callers get an immediate error or fallback; the sick dependency gets breathing room
After the cooldown (for example 30 s) a few trial calls are allowed
Trial calls succeed: breaker closes and traffic resumes. If they fail it reopens and the cooldown restarts

deep.title: Tuning and the resilience toolbox
deep.body:
Parameters: failure-rate threshold (or consecutive failures), minimum calls before judging (avoid opening on 1 of 2), sliding window (count-based or time-based), slow-call threshold (treat latency above X as failure), open-state wait, and the number of half-open probe calls.

What counts as failure: timeouts, 5xx, connection errors; not 4xx caused by caller mistakes.

Companions:

- Timeouts: every call has one; they define what 'slow' means.
- Bulkheads: separate thread pools, connection pools or semaphores per dependency so one slow dependency cannot use all capacity.
- Retries with backoff and jitter, inside the breaker, with a retry budget.
- Fallbacks: cached or default data, a degraded feature, or a queued write. Decide what the user sees when open.
- Load shedding and rate limits on the server side.

Per-instance vs shared state: each client instance usually keeps its own breaker (no shared dependency); for sidecars and meshes (Envoy outlier detection) ejection decisions are made per upstream host.

Observability: emit state changes and rejected-call counts, alert when a breaker is open, and dashboard them next to the dependency's error rate.

deep.title: Backoff formulas and retry amplification
deep.body:
Exponential backoff: delay = min(cap, base × 2^attempt). Without randomness, clients that failed together retry together.

Jitter strategies (AWS Architecture Blog analysis):

- Full jitter: sleep = random(0, min(cap, base × 2^attempt)). Fewest total calls and best spreading; the default recommendation.
- Equal jitter: sleep = half + random(0, half).
- Decorrelated jitter: sleep = min(cap, random(base, previous_sleep × 3)).

Amplification: with k attempts per layer and d layers, one user request can become k^d downstream requests (3 layers × 3 attempts = 27). Retry at one layer only, usually the edge, and use a retry budget (for example retries may add at most 10% extra load, tracked as a token bucket refilled by successes).

Deadline propagation: pass the remaining time budget downstream (gRPC deadlines), so a request that cannot finish in time is dropped instead of doing wasted work.

Idempotency: retry only operations that are safe to repeat or carry an idempotency key.

Server protections: load shedding (reject early when queue time exceeds a limit, return 503 with Retry-After), adaptive concurrency limits, and admission control by priority so critical traffic survives. Hedged requests (send a second copy after the p95 latency) reduce tail latency but add load, so budget them too.

deep.title: Choosing B and r, and variable cost
deep.body:
To enforce 'L requests per W seconds on average with bursts up to B': set r = L / W and capacity B. B = L gives a window-like behavior with refill; B = 1 gives smooth pacing (one request every 1/r seconds); a larger B tolerates spikier clients.

Example: 100 requests/minute, burst 20: r = 100/60 = 1.67 tokens/s, B = 20. A client idle for 12 seconds has 20 tokens, can fire 20 at once, then gets one every 0.6 s.

Variable cost: charge cost tokens per request (search = 5, read = 1, LLM call = estimated tokens / 1000). The bucket then limits resource consumption, not just request count.

Hierarchical buckets: charge several buckets at once (per-user, per-tenant, global) and allow only if all pass; refund earlier buckets if a later one rejects.

Implementation tips: store floats or use integer micro-tokens; refill lazily on access, never with a timer per key; set a TTL on idle keys; return the wait time for Retry-After.

deep.title: Algorithms and when each fails
deep.body:
Round robin: next server in turn. Ignores load, so long requests pile up on unlucky servers. Weighted round robin handles unequal machines.

Random: simple; with many requests approaches even load but has variance.

Least connections: send to the server with the fewest open connections. Adapts to slow requests; needs connection tracking.

Power of two choices: pick two servers at random and send to the less loaded. Gives an exponential improvement in maximum load over pure random with almost no coordination; used widely at scale.

Least response time / peak EWMA: weight by observed latency.

IP/consistent hash: same client or key to same server; gives affinity and cache locality; bounded-load variants cap overload.

Health: active checks (probe endpoints), passive checks (eject on errors, outlier detection), slow start for new servers, connection draining on removal.

Layers: L4 (TCP/UDP, fast, no HTTP awareness) vs L7 (routes by path/header, terminates TLS, retries, canary weights). Global load balancing: DNS (GeoDNS, latency-based routing; TTL delays failover), anycast (same IP announced from many sites, routed by BGP).

High availability: LB pairs with VRRP/floating IP or managed LBs; never a single instance.

deep.title: Fan-out math and the hybrid design
deep.body:
Fan-out on write cost: writes per post = number of followers F. At 100 posts/s and average F = 200 that is 20,000 timeline inserts/s, fine. One celebrity with F = 50 million posting once causes 50 million inserts: at 100k inserts/s that takes 500 seconds and floods the system. Fan-out on read cost: read must query the recent posts of every followee (say 300) and merge: 300 lookups per timeline load.

Hybrid: push for authors with F below a threshold (for example 10,000), pull for the rest. On read, merge the precomputed timeline (a capped list, say the last 800 post ids in Redis) with recent posts of the few celebrities the user follows, then rank.

Storage: timeline entry = (post_id, score). 800 entries × 16 bytes × 500M users = 6.4 TB, so skip inactive users (build their timeline lazily on next login) and cap lengths.

Other details: store post bodies once and hydrate by id; use queues to fan out asynchronously and rate limit fan-out workers; handle deletes with tombstones and filter at read; rank with a feature store; use cursor pagination for stable scrolling.

Same pattern elsewhere: notifications, activity feeds, chat group delivery, webhooks to many subscribers.

deep.title: Geohash, quadtree, S2 and H3 in detail
deep.body:
Geohash: interleaves latitude and longitude bits and encodes them in base32. Longer prefix means a smaller cell (5 chars about 4.9 km × 4.9 km, 6 chars about 1.2 km × 0.6 km, 7 chars about 150 m). Points sharing a prefix are near, so a prefix range scan on an ordinary index finds candidates. Boundary issue: two close points can have different prefixes, so query the cell and its 8 neighbors, then filter by true distance (haversine).

Quadtree: recursively split a square into four children when it holds more than K points. Dense areas get deep, small cells; sparse areas stay coarse. Search descends to the query point and expands to neighbors. Lives in memory; shard by region and rebuild or update incrementally.

S2 (Google): maps the sphere onto a cube and uses a Hilbert curve to order cells, giving cells of near-uniform size at each of 30 levels and a 64-bit cell id; good locality and region covering.

H3 (Uber): hexagonal grid; each cell has 6 equidistant neighbors, which makes radius queries and smoothing simple.

Haversine distance: a = sin²(Δφ/2) + cos φ1 × cos φ2 × sin²(Δλ/2); d = 2R × asin(sqrt(a)) with R = 6371 km.

Ride-hailing design: drivers send a location every 3-5 seconds; store the latest position per driver in Redis (geo commands or cell sets with TTL); matching queries cell and neighbors, filters by availability, ranks by ETA from a routing service. Never write every ping to the primary database; stream them to Kafka for analytics.

deep.title: Choosing the transport and scaling connections
deep.body:
Short polling: client asks every N seconds. Simple, wasteful, latency up to N.

Long polling: server holds the request until data arrives or a timeout. Near real-time with plain HTTP; reconnect overhead.

Server-sent events (SSE): one-way server to client over HTTP, automatic reconnect with Last-Event-ID, great for notifications and LLM token streaming; works through most proxies; browsers limit connections per domain on HTTP/1.1.

WebSocket: full-duplex over a single TCP connection after an HTTP upgrade. Best for chat, multiplayer, collaboration. Needs heartbeats, backoff-on-reconnect, sticky routing or a pub/sub layer, and care with proxies and load balancers.

WebRTC: peer-to-peer media and data over UDP with STUN/TURN for NAT traversal; for voice and video.

Scaling connection servers: each connection costs memory (roughly 10-50 KB tuned) and a file descriptor; a tuned node can hold hundreds of thousands. Keep the connection tier thin: authenticate, subscribe to channels, push. Route messages with pub/sub (Redis, NATS, Kafka): the sender publishes to a channel and every connection server with subscribers delivers. Keep a presence map (user to connection server) with TTL refreshed by heartbeats.

Reliability: assign each message a per-channel sequence number; clients ack and resume from last seen sequence after reconnect; dedupe by message id; reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter so a deploy does not cause a thundering herd; drain connections gracefully on deploy.

deep.title: Snowflake layout and capacity math
deep.body:
64-bit id: 1 sign bit (unused), 41 bits timestamp in milliseconds since a custom epoch, 10 bits machine/worker id, 12 bits sequence.

Capacity: 2^41 ms is about 69.7 years of ids per epoch. 12 sequence bits give 4,096 ids per millisecond per worker, about 4.1 million per second per worker. 10 worker bits allow 1,024 workers, so cluster-wide throughput reaches about 4 billion ids per second.

Worker id assignment: from a coordination service (ZooKeeper/etcd lease) or config; two workers sharing an id produce duplicates, so assign carefully and handle restarts.

Clock issues: NTP can step the clock back. Strategies: refuse to generate until the clock catches up; keep using the last timestamp and increment the sequence; or fail loudly. Monitor drift.

Ordering: ids are roughly time-sorted across workers (ordering within the same millisecond across workers is arbitrary), which gives index locality and lets you sort by id instead of by timestamp.

UUID options: v4 is 122 random bits (collision odds negligible, poor B-tree locality); v7 puts a 48-bit unix ms timestamp first then random bits (sortable, locality); ULID is a 48-bit time plus 80 random bits in a 26-char base32 string.

Base62 short codes: 62^7 is about 3.5 trillion, enough for most URL shorteners with 7 characters. Encode a unique counter or Snowflake id; do not truncate hashes without handling collisions.

flows.title: Transactional outbox end to end
flows.hint: One database transaction, then a relay, then idempotent consumers.

steps.note: Handle 'place order'
In ONE transaction: insert the order row and an OrderPlaced row into the outbox table. Both commit or neither does
Relay polls unsent outbox rows (or Debezium reads the WAL) and publishes them
Event appended to the topic keyed by order_id. If the relay crashes after publishing but before marking sent, it republishes: duplicates are possible
Consumer checks a processed-events table in the same transaction as its effect, so a duplicate is ignored

deep.title: Idempotency in detail
deep.body:
API idempotency keys: the client generates a unique key per logical operation (a UUID) and sends it with each retry. The server, in one transaction, inserts (key, request_hash, status) with a unique constraint, performs the work, and stores the response. A duplicate request finds the key and returns the stored response; the same key with a different request body is rejected. Concurrent duplicates: the unique insert makes one proceed and the other wait or get 409. Expire keys after a window (24 hours is common).

Consumer idempotency: store processed message ids with the effect in the same transaction; or make the effect naturally idempotent (upsert by id, set-to-value instead of increment, version checks).

Ordering: events for one entity must be applied in order; key by entity id. Include a version or sequence number and ignore stale events.

Outbox operations: relay by polling (SELECT ... WHERE sent = false ORDER BY id LIMIT n FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) scales across several relays; clean up sent rows on a schedule; monitor outbox age as an SLI.

CDC details: Debezium on Postgres reads the logical replication stream via a replication slot (watch for slots retaining WAL when the connector is down); emits before/after row images; handle schema evolution with a schema registry; initial snapshot then streaming.
